question: A 21-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of right leg pain. The pain is worse while walking and improves when resting. Eight months ago, she was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism and was started on warfarin. Anticoagulant therapy was discontinued two months ago. Her mother had systemic lupus erythematosus. On examination, her right calf is diffusely erythematous, swollen, and tender. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. On duplex ultrasonography, the right popliteal vein is not compressible. Laboratory studies show an elevated serum level of D-dimer and insensitivity to activated protein C. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "History of pulmonary embolism" -> "Started on warfarin" -> "Discontinued anticoagulant therapy" -> "Increased risk of recurrent thrombosis" -> "Right leg pain, erythema, swelling, tenderness" -> "Suspicion of deep vein thrombosis" -> "Duplex ultrasonography showing non-compressible right popliteal vein" -> "Elevated D-dimer levels" -> "Insensitivity to activated protein C" -> "Likely to have a hypercoagulable state" -> "Further evaluation for genetic causes of hypercoagulability" -> "Most likely to show mutation of coagulation factor V" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Family history of systemic lupus erythematosus" -> "Possible genetic predisposition to autoimmune diseases" -> "Increased likelihood of autoimmune conditions in the patient" -> "Possible association with protein S deficiency" -> "Further evaluation for protein S deficiency" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's presentation with a history of pulmonary embolism, recent leg pain, erythema, swelling, and tenderness in the right calf, along with a non-compressible right popliteal vein on ultrasound, elevated D-dimer, and insensitivity to activated protein C suggests a high likelihood of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Given the family history of systemic lupus erythematosus, further evaluation is likely to reveal a mutation of coagulation factor V (Factor V Leiden mutation) as a common genetic risk factor for DVT.
